architects.name: Andrea Palladio
architects.bio: Born in Padua and trained as a stonemason, Palladio became the most influential architect of the Renaissance. His treatise The Four Books of Architecture (1570) spread his symmetrical, temple-fronted villas across Europe and the Americas, giving rise to Palladianism.

architects.name: Vincenzo Scamozzi
architects.bio: Born in Vicenza, Scamozzi inherited several of Palladio's unfinished projects after the master's death in 1580, among them the Teatro Olimpico and La Rotonda, where he designed the lower, Pantheon-like dome. His treatise L'idea della architettura universale (1615) and his only pupil, Baldassarre Longhena, carried Palladian ideas into the Venetian Baroque.

drawings.label: Main floor plan
drawings.alt: Square floor plan with an identical portico on each of its four sides and a circular hall at the centre
drawings.credit: Ottavio Bertotti Scamozzi, engraving, 1778 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Cross section
drawings.alt: Section through a raised villa showing a central domed hall rising above the surrounding rooms
drawings.credit: Ottavio Bertotti Scamozzi, engraving, 1778 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

image.alt: Looking up into a frescoed dome with an oculus at its centre
image.credit: Photo: Andrek02 · CC0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: The whole house turns around a single domed, circular hall.

hints.text: Four identical temple fronts face the four directions, so this hilltop house has no back.

image.alt: Cream-coloured villa on a lawn, with temple porticoes on two visible sides and a low tiled dome
image.credit: Photo: Hans A. Rosbach · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Begun in 1567 on a hilltop outside Vicenza for the retired cleric Paolo Almerico, La Rotonda is a perfectly symmetrical square block with a portico on every side and a domed hall at its heart. Palladio treated a private house like an ancient temple, and the result became one of the most copied buildings in Western architecture.
keyFeatures: Square plan with four identical Ionic porticoes
Central circular hall under a dome
Symmetry on both axes
Raised on a hill to command views on every side
funFacts: Palladio died in 1580; Vincenzo Scamozzi completed the villa and replaced the planned high dome with a lower one, open to the sky through an oculus like the Pantheon in Rome.
It inspired buildings from Chiswick House in London to country houses across Britain and America.
It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site 'City of Vicenza and the Palladian Villas of the Veneto'.

architects.name: Francesco Borromini
architects.bio: A stonemason's son from Bissone on Lake Lugano, Borromini spent his career in Rome, where his restless geometry and rippling walls made him the great rival of Gian Lorenzo Bernini. He built few, mostly small, churches, yet his inventive use of geometry shaped Baroque architecture across Europe.

drawings.label: Church and courtyard plan
drawings.alt: Plan of a six-pointed star formed by two overlapping triangles, with rounded and angled recesses at its points
drawings.credit: Francesco Borromini, Opera del Caval. Francesco Boromino, 1720 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: Section through the dome
drawings.alt: Cut-away view of a tall centralized church: the walls rise into a ribbed dome topped by a slender lantern
drawings.credit: Francesco Borromini, Opera del Caval. Francesco Boromino, 1720 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

image.alt: Looking up white walls that flow without a break into a star-patterned dome
image.credit: Photo: Hugo DK · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: The walls flow upward into the dome without a break.

hints.text: The church closes the end of a courtyard belonging to the city's old university.

image.alt: Concave church front at the end of an arcaded courtyard, crowned by a spiralling lantern
image.credit: Photo: Pedro P. Palazzo · CC BY 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A spiral lantern crowns the dome.

summary.description: Borromini built this university church inside the existing courtyard of the Palazzo della Sapienza in Rome. Its plan grows from two interlocking equilateral triangles, and the star-shaped walls continue straight up into the dome, making the whole interior read as a single sculpted space.
keyFeatures: Star plan from two interlocking triangles
Walls and dome form one continuous surface
Almost colourless white interior that puts form first
Spiral lantern above a stepped dome
funFacts: The plan is often said to evoke a bee, the heraldic emblem of Pope Urban VIII's Barberini family.
Borromini was appointed architect of the Sapienza in 1632, reportedly on Bernini's recommendation.
Construction spanned the reigns of three popes, each of whom left his emblems on the building.

architects.name: Thomas Jefferson
architects.bio: Third President of the United States and principal author of the Declaration of Independence, Jefferson was also a self-taught architect. Learning largely from Palladio's books, he promoted classical architecture as a model for the new republic and designed the Virginia State Capitol and the University of Virginia.

drawings.label: First floor plan
drawings.alt: Symmetrical house plan with porticoes front and back, a central hall and parlour, and octagonal rooms at the corners
drawings.credit: Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS VA-241), measured drawing, 1989–92 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

drawings.label: South elevation
drawings.alt: Side elevation of a house with three tall arched windows below a balustraded roof and a low dome
drawings.credit: Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS VA-241), measured drawing, 1989–92 · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

image.alt: Hall wall hung with antlers, maps and a library ladder above a marble bust
image.credit: Photo: Frypie · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: The entrance hall doubled as a museum of fossils, maps and expedition finds.

hints.text: Its owner spent four decades designing, demolishing and rebuilding it.

image.alt: Red-brick house with a white columned portico and a low octagonal dome, seen across a lawn
image.credit: Photo: YF12s · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: This façade appears on a US coin.

summary.description: Jefferson began his hilltop plantation house in 1768 and spent forty years reshaping it, adding an octagonal dome after seeing the latest Neoclassical buildings in Paris. Built and maintained largely by enslaved people, it is today presented both as an architectural landmark and as a place to confront the history of slavery in the United States.
keyFeatures: Low octagonal dome over the west front
Temple-like porticoes in the manner of Palladio
Designed to look like a single storey, hiding the upper floors
Service wings tucked under terraces in the hillside
funFacts: The west front is pictured on the back of the US five-cent coin.
It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the University of Virginia, which Jefferson also designed.
Jefferson learned architecture largely from Palladio's Four Books, and the porticoes and proportions show it.

architects.name: Le Corbusier
architects.bio: Born Charles-Édouard Jeanneret in La Chaux-de-Fonds, Switzerland, he took the name Le Corbusier in Paris and became one of the founders of modern architecture. His writings, buildings and city plans, from the Five Points of Architecture to the Unité d'Habitation, shaped twentieth-century design worldwide.

architects.name: Pierre Jeanneret
architects.bio: Le Corbusier's cousin and partner for nearly two decades, Pierre Jeanneret co-signed the firm's houses of the 1920s and 1930s. He later spent fifteen years in India building the new city of Chandigarh, where his furniture designs have since become collectors' pieces.

drawings.label: Ground floor plan
drawings.alt: Square grid of slender columns with a curved glazed entrance hall at one end

drawings.label: First floor plan
drawings.alt: Square upper floor wrapped around an open-air terrace, with a ramp at the centre

drawings.label: Longitudinal section
drawings.alt: Section showing a ramp rising through three levels to a roof garden

hints.text: A ramp climbs through the middle of the house, from the entrance hall up to a roof garden.
The curve of the glazed ground floor was set by the turning circle of a car.
The house stands alone in a meadow in a western suburb of Paris, lifted off the grass on slender columns.

summary.description: Designed as a weekend house for Pierre and Eugénie Savoye, the villa is a white box lifted on slender columns above a meadow outside Paris. It is the fullest demonstration of Le Corbusier's Five Points of Architecture and a defining work of the International Style.
keyFeatures: Pilotis lifting the house off the ground
Free plan, unconstrained by load-bearing walls
Free façade, independent of the structure
Long horizontal ribbon windows
Roof garden replacing the ground lost below
funFacts: The family named it 'Les Heures Claires' (The Bright Hours).
Persistent roof leaks made the house hard to live in, and the Savoyes complained repeatedly.
After years of neglect and a threat of demolition, it was listed as a French historic monument in 1965.

architects.name: Louis Kahn
architects.bio: Born on the island of Saaremaa in present-day Estonia and raised in Philadelphia, Kahn found his voice late, in his fifties. His monumental buildings of concrete, brick and light, including the Kimbell Art Museum and the National Assembly of Bangladesh, made him one of the most revered architects of the twentieth century.

drawings.label: Site plan
drawings.alt: Two long parallel wings on either side of an open plaza, ending at a cliff edge

drawings.label: Cross section
drawings.alt: Section through stacked laboratory floors alternating with shallower service floors

image.alt: Shaded passage of raw concrete, its timber-marked walls dotted with small round holes
image.credit: Photo: Beyond My Ken · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Raw, board-formed concrete; the holes left by the formwork ties are kept on show.

hints.text: The client asked for a place worthy of a visit by Picasso.

image.alt: Empty stone plaza between two concrete wings, a thin water channel running toward the ocean at sunset
image.credit: Photo: TheNose · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Two mirror-image wings frame an empty plaza that opens to the Pacific.

summary.description: Commissioned by Jonas Salk, developer of the polio vaccine, the institute sits on cliffs above the Pacific. Two symmetrical laboratory wings flank a travertine plaza cut by a narrow channel of water running toward the ocean, one of the most celebrated outdoor spaces in modern architecture.
keyFeatures: Board-formed concrete with exposed form-tie holes
Travertine plaza split by a central water channel
Service floors between the labs for flexible layouts
Teak-clad studies angled toward the ocean
funFacts: Mexican architect Luis Barragán persuaded Kahn to leave the plaza bare instead of planting a garden, calling it a façade to the sky.
The water channel lines up with the setting sun around the equinoxes.
Kahn's plan also included residences and a meeting house, but only the laboratories were built.

name: Igreja de São Francisco de Assis (Ouro Preto)
aliases: Igreja de São Francisco de Assis
Church of Saint Francis of Assisi
São Francisco de Assis de Ouro Preto

architects.name: Antônio Francisco Lisboa
architects.bio: Son of a Portuguese architect and an enslaved African woman, Aleijadinho ('the little cripple') became the greatest artist of colonial Brazil, carving soapstone and wood across the gold-mining towns of Minas Gerais. A degenerative illness left him disabled, yet he kept working; his twelve soapstone prophets at Congonhas are his best-known sculptures.

image.alt: Painted ceiling of a church nave: a sky full of figures framed by painted architecture
image.credit: Photo: Rezende1968 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: The nave ceiling, painted by Manuel da Costa Ataíde.

hints.text: Its circular bell towers were a novelty among the region's churches, and its frontispiece is carved in local soapstone.

image.alt: White church with round bell towers and ornate stone carving around a green door
image.credit: Photo: Paulo Bueno · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Built for the Third Order of Saint Francis in Ouro Preto, the gold-rush capital of Minas Gerais, this church is the masterpiece of Aleijadinho, who designed both the building and much of its carving. Its curving façade, round towers and soapstone reliefs make it the defining work of the Barroco Mineiro, the late, Rococo-tinged Baroque of Brazil's mining towns.
keyFeatures: Circular bell towers set back from the façade
Soapstone frontispiece with a relief of Saint Francis receiving the stigmata
Oculus filled with a carved relief instead of a window
Nave ceiling painted by Manuel da Costa Ataíde
funFacts: The Third Order asked Lisbon for permission to build in 1752; approval only came in 1771, years after work had begun under a provisional licence.
Ouro Preto's historic centre is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

name: Mosteiro de São Bento
aliases: Mosteiro de São Bento do Rio de Janeiro

architects.name: Francisco Frias de Mesquita
architects.bio: A Portuguese military engineer sent to colonial Brazil, Frias de Mesquita designed fortifications and buildings along the coast. In 1617 he drew up the plans for São Bento in the plain Mannerist manner then current in Portugal.

architects.name: Frei Bernardo de São Bento Correia de Souza
architects.bio: A Benedictine friar and architect active in colonial Rio de Janeiro and one of the main figures behind the monastery's construction. He altered the original plan while it was being built, turning the single-nave church into one with three naves.

image.alt: Plain white church front with two pointed towers and three arched entrances
image.credit: Photo: Klayton Aurélio de Oliveira · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A sober front of white walls and grey stone, on a hill above the port.

hints.text: It was paid for with income from sugar-cane estates given to the monks, and built by enslaved labourers.

image.alt: Church nave lined almost entirely with gilded carved woodwork
image.credit: Photo: Rafael.carvalhosa · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Inside, almost every surface is covered in gilded carving.

summary.description: Planned in 1617 and begun in 1633 on a hill overlooking Rio de Janeiro's harbour, the Benedictine monastery hides one of the richest Baroque interiors in Brazil behind a sober Mannerist façade. The church was enlarged to three naves during construction, and from the late 17th century its walls and vaults were covered in gilded carving.
keyFeatures: Mannerist façade with three entrance arches and a triangular pediment
Nave and chapels lined with gilded woodcarving (talha dourada)
Carving that runs from late Baroque to Rococo
Cloister completed in 1755
funFacts: Much of the carving in the nave and chancel was designed by the Benedictine Frei Domingos da Conceição (1643–1718).
The cloister was designed by the military engineer José Fernandes Pinto Alpoim and finished in 1755.

name: Theatro Municipal do Rio de Janeiro
aliases: Municipal Theatre of Rio de Janeiro

architects.name: Francisco de Oliveira Passos
architects.bio: An engineer and later politician, the son of Rio's reforming mayor Francisco Pereira Passos. Under the pseudonym 'Áquila' he won the city's competition for a new municipal theatre.

architects.name: Albert Guilbert
architects.bio: French architect who worked with Oliveira Passos on the theatre's design, which takes Charles Garnier's Paris Opéra as its model.

image.alt: Gilded eagle with spread wings on top of a green and gold dome
image.credit: Photo: Dennis G. Jarvis · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A gilded eagle crowns one of the domes.

hints.text: It was built in four and a half years, from 1905 to 1909, on a foundation of 1,180 wooden piles driven into waterlogged ground.

image.alt: Black-and-white street of wet cobblestones leading to an ornate domed building
image.credit: Photo: Antonio Donioli · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Rio's opera house was the showpiece of the city's Parisian-style remodelling in the early 1900s, when the new Avenida Central was cut through the old centre. Its eclectic, richly sculpted design follows Charles Garnier's Paris Opéra, and it opened in July 1909 with seats for 1,739 people.
keyFeatures: Eclectic façade modelled on the Paris Opéra
Green and gilded domes crowned by eagles
Names of European and Brazilian artists inscribed on the outer walls
Foundation of 1,180 wooden piles
funFacts: The winning design was entered under the pseudonym 'Áquila'.
President Nilo Peçanha inaugurated it on 14 July 1909.
It faces Cinelândia square, near the National Library and the National Museum of Fine Arts.

name: Palácio Gustavo Capanema
aliases: Ministry of Education and Health Building

architects.name: Lúcio Costa
architects.bio: Costa led the team that designed the Ministry and became the leading theorist of Brazilian modernism. He is best known for the Plano Piloto, the master plan of Brasília.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

architects.name: Affonso Eduardo Reidy
architects.bio: Son of an English father and a Brazilian mother, Reidy trained in Rio de Janeiro and spent much of his career designing for the city, from the Pedregulho housing estate to the Museum of Modern Art in Flamengo Park.

architects.name: Carlos Leão
architects.bio: Rio-born architect, painter and watercolourist, and a member of Lúcio Costa's team for the Ministry of Education and Health.

architects.name: Jorge Machado Moreira
architects.bio: A member of the Ministry team, Moreira later led the planning and design of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro's campus on Fundão Island.

architects.name: Ernani Vasconcellos
architects.bio: Architect, painter and muralist from Rio de Janeiro, and the youngest member of the Ministry team.

image.alt: Wall of blue and white tiles with flowing shapes and stars, behind slender columns
image.credit: Photo: Wagner Tamanaha · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Blue and white tiles under the raised block, a nod to Portuguese colonial azulejos.

hints.text: The young Brazilian team invited Le Corbusier to advise them on the design in 1936.

image.alt: Tall office slab whose façade is covered in adjustable horizontal sun-shades
image.credit: Photo: Imagens AMB · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Adjustable sun-shades on the north façade.

summary.description: Designed in 1935–36 and completed in 1945 for Brazil's new Ministry of Education and Health, this fifteen-storey slab was the country's first great modernist public building. It is raised on pilotis above an open ground floor, shaded by adjustable brises-soleil, and decorated with azulejo tiles, Portinari murals and gardens by Roberto Burle Marx.
keyFeatures: Slab raised on tall pilotis above a public ground floor
Adjustable brises-soleil on the north façade, the first system of its kind
Blue and white azulejo murals
Gardens by Roberto Burle Marx
funFacts: Oscar Niemeyer began on the project as an intern in Lúcio Costa's office.
It was the first modernist public building in the Americas, larger than anything Le Corbusier himself had built by then.
The tile murals outside and the paintings inside are by Cândido Portinari.

name: Igreja de São Francisco de Assis da Pampulha
aliases: Church of Saint Francis of Assisi (Pampulha)

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

image.alt: Curved concrete vault beside a tall lattice bell tower
image.credit: Photo: Nicolas de Camaret · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A parabolic concrete vault and a separate lattice bell tower.

hints.text: Church authorities refused for years to consecrate it, objecting to its form and to a mural showing a dog beside Saint Francis.

image.alt: Row of white parabolic vaults with a blue and white tile mural, beside a lattice tower
image.credit: Photo: Camilla Vitoria Machado · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: The last building of the Pampulha ensemble that Niemeyer designed for Juscelino Kubitschek, then mayor of Belo Horizonte, this small chapel abandons the slab-on-pilotis formula for a row of parabolic concrete vaults that are structure and enclosure at once. Its free curves announced a distinctly Brazilian modernism.
keyFeatures: Parabolic reinforced-concrete vaults, a form then used for hangars
Vaults acting as both structure and walls
Freestanding lattice bell tower
Tile murals by Cândido Portinari and Paulo Werneck
funFacts: Inside, Portinari's fourteen Stations of the Cross are considered among his most important works.
The structure was calculated by the engineer Joaquim Cardozo, Niemeyer's long-time collaborator.
The Pampulha Modern Ensemble became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2016.

architects.name: Lina Bo Bardi
architects.bio: Born Achillina Bo in Rome, she moved to Brazil in 1946 with her husband, the critic and dealer Pietro Maria Bardi. Fascinated by Brazilian popular culture, she joined modernist rigour to a raw, humane architecture, from MASP to SESC Pompéia.

image.alt: Light steel staircase rising between thin columns into a forest canopy
image.credit: Photo: Igor Marotti · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: A light steel stair rises from the forest floor to the glazed living floor.

hints.text: It was its architect's first built work, finished the year she became a naturalized Brazilian.

image.alt: Glass-walled house raised on slender stilts among dense trees
image.credit: Photo: LeoINN · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Lina Bo Bardi built this house for herself and her husband in 1951 on a steep plot in what was then a remnant of Atlantic Forest on the edge of São Paulo. A glass-walled living floor floats on slender pilotis above the slope, letting the landscape flow beneath it; today the forest has grown back and hides the house from view.
keyFeatures: Glass-walled living floor on thin steel pilotis
Light stair rising from the garden
Landscape flowing under the raised house
Forest regrown around the building
funFacts: It was one of the first three houses in the then-new Morumbi neighbourhood.
It now houses the institute that looks after the archive of Lina Bo Bardi and Pietro Maria Bardi.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

image.alt: Black-and-white view of slender, curving white columns tapering to points
image.credit: Photo: Unknown photographer · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Its columns taper to fine points at top and bottom.

hints.text: Its name comes from a question its client asked: what is the new capital, if not the dawn of a new day for Brazil?

image.alt: Long, low glass palace behind a colonnade of curving white columns, reflected in a pool at dusk
image.credit: Photo: MTur Destinos · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Built in about fourteen months, from April 1957 to June 1958, the official residence of the President of Brazil was one of the first buildings of the new capital. A long glass box sits behind a portico of sculptural white columns whose curves became a symbol of Brasília.
keyFeatures: Glass box set back behind a colonnade
Curving columns tapering to fine points
Reflecting pool in front
Long, low proportions near the shore of Lake Paranoá
funFacts: Every Brazilian president since Juscelino Kubitschek has lived there.
A golden wall inside carries a 1956 quotation by Kubitschek about the new capital.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

image.alt: Black-and-white construction site with a long platform and the base of a dome
image.credit: Photo: Arquivo Nacional (Brazil) · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Under construction in the late 1950s.

hints.text: The low dome shelters one chamber of the legislature; the upturned bowl, the other.

image.alt: Twin office towers rising between a dome and an upturned bowl on a long platform, beside a pool
image.credit: Photo: Senado Federal · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Inaugurated with the new capital in 1960, Brazil's parliament closes the Esplanade of Ministries at the Square of the Three Powers. Niemeyer set the two houses on a long horizontal platform, the Senate under a dome and the Chamber of Deputies in an upturned bowl, with twin 28-storey office towers rising between them.
keyFeatures: Horizontal platform whose roof is a raised plaza
Dome over the Federal Senate
Upturned bowl over the Chamber of Deputies
Twin office towers linked to form an H
funFacts: In Rio de Janeiro the two houses had sat in separate buildings; Brasília joined them in one palace.
The structure was designed by the engineer Joaquim Cardozo.
Brasília is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

image.alt: Close-up of a towering curved façade wrapped in continuous horizontal concrete bands
image.credit: Photo: Paul R. Burley · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Horizontal concrete sun-breakers wrap the whole façade.

hints.text: It has so many residents that the postal service gave it a postcode of its own.

image.alt: Wavy residential tower with horizontal bands rising above the city
image.credit: Photo: MTur Destinos · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Conceived for the fourth centenary of São Paulo, Copan is a single sinuous slab, 115 metres tall, holding 1,160 apartments, from studios to three-bedroom flats, above a shopping arcade. Begun in 1952 and finished only in 1966, it houses residents of very different incomes in one building.
keyFeatures: S-shaped plan
Continuous horizontal brise-soleil
1,160 apartments in six blocks
Ground-floor shopping gallery open to the street
funFacts: Its reinforced-concrete structure is the largest in Brazil.
Niemeyer was personally responsible for the sinuous façade; the project was developed with the architect Carlos Lemos.

name: Museu de Arte Moderna do Rio de Janeiro
aliases: Museum of Modern Art of Rio de Janeiro

architects.name: Affonso Eduardo Reidy
architects.bio: Son of an English father and a Brazilian mother, Reidy trained in Rio de Janeiro and spent much of his career designing for the city, from the Pedregulho housing estate to the Museum of Modern Art in Flamengo Park.

image.alt: Raw concrete frames slanting outwards beside a glazed gallery
image.credit: Photo: Pedro Mendonça · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Slanted concrete frames carry the galleries.

hints.text: A fire in 1978 destroyed about 90% of its collection, including works by Picasso, Miró, Magritte and Dalí.

image.alt: Long concrete building held by a row of V-shaped frames above a garden pool
image.credit: Photo: Halley Pacheco de Oliveira · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Set in Flamengo Park, on land reclaimed from Guanabara Bay, the Museum of Modern Art is Affonso Eduardo Reidy's masterpiece. Its long exhibition block is carried by a row of V-shaped concrete frames, freeing the galleries of columns and opening the ground floor to views of the gardens by Roberto Burle Marx.
keyFeatures: Exhibition block carried by V-shaped concrete frames
Column-free galleries
Ground floor open between park and bay
Gardens by Roberto Burle Marx
funFacts: The school block opened first, in 1958; the exhibition block was completed in 1967.
Reidy's partner, the engineer Carmen Portinho, was chief engineer on the project.

name: Museu de Arte de São Paulo
aliases: Museu de Arte de São Paulo Assis Chateaubriand

architects.name: Lina Bo Bardi
architects.bio: Born Achillina Bo in Rome, she moved to Brazil in 1946 with her husband, the critic and dealer Pietro Maria Bardi. Fascinated by Brazilian popular culture, she joined modernist rigour to a raw, humane architecture, from MASP to SESC Pompéia.

image.alt: Aerial view of a long roof with two red beams spanning across it, beside a busy avenue
image.credit: Photo: ProtoplasmaKid · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Two great red beams run the length of the building.

hints.text: Its collection of European art is considered one of the finest in the Southern Hemisphere.

image.alt: Glass-walled gallery box held up between two red-painted concrete frames
image.credit: Photo: Boaventuravinicius · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: On the site of the old Trianon belvedere on Avenida Paulista, Lina Bo Bardi lifted the museum's galleries into a glass and concrete box hung between two great frames. Beneath it, a covered public plaza about 74 metres long is left open to the city.
keyFeatures: Gallery box spanning about 74 metres between two pairs of pillars
Free public plaza beneath (the vão livre)
Exposed concrete and glass
Paintings shown on transparent easels
funFacts: Bo Bardi displayed the paintings on glass and concrete easels so they seemed to float in the gallery; the museum brought them back in 2015.
The museum opened in 1947 in a downtown building and moved here in 1968.
Queen Elizabeth II attended its inauguration in 1968.

name: Edifício da FAU-USP
aliases: Faculdade de Arquitetura e Urbanismo da USP
Faculty of Architecture and Urbanism, University of São Paulo

architects.name: Vilanova Artigas
architects.bio: Born in Curitiba, Artigas became the founding figure of the Paulista School and a long-time teacher at the University of São Paulo's architecture faculty, whose building he designed. The military regime removed him from teaching in 1969.

architects.name: Carlos Cascaldi
architects.bio: São Paulo architect, a former student of Vilanova Artigas and his partner throughout the 1950s, and co-author of the faculty building.

image.alt: Tapering concrete column under the edge of a massive raw-concrete block
image.credit: Photo: Matheus Carvalho Teixeira · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: The heavy concrete block rests on slender, tapering columns.

hints.text: A sequence of gentle ramps links all its floors around a great central hall under a skylit roof.

image.alt: Massive concrete box with a deep overhang on tapered columns, behind a lawn
image.credit: Photo: Lombana · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Inaugurated in 1969, Vilanova Artigas's building for the University of São Paulo's architecture school gathers its studios under a single concrete roof pierced by skylights. Ramps join the staggered levels around a central hall, expressing Artigas's idea of the school as an open, democratic space.
keyFeatures: Single roof of concrete coffers with skylights
Ramps connecting staggered levels
Great central hall as a meeting space
Heavy concrete block on slender tapered columns
funFacts: Artigas also helped create the school's curriculum, giving equal weight to technique, history and design.
The military regime removed Artigas from teaching in 1969, the year the building opened.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

image.alt: Crown of curved white concrete ribs seen across a glass roof
image.credit: Photo: Fwsbsb2 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: From outside, the ribs rise like a crown above a glass roof.

hints.text: Bronze statues of the four Evangelists stand at its entrance.

image.alt: Circular building of sixteen curved white concrete ribs gathered at the top, with glass between them
image.credit: Photo: Agência Brasília · CC BY 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: A hyperboloid of sixteen curved concrete columns, each weighing about 90 tonnes, rises from a circular base like hands reaching towards the sky. Visitors enter through a dark, low passage and emerge into a nave filled with coloured light.
keyFeatures: Hyperboloid of 16 concrete columns
Glass between the ribs, with stained glass by Marianne Peretti (1990)
Entrance through a low, dark passage
Reflecting pool around the building
funFacts: Three angels by Alfredo Ceschiatti hang from steel cables over the nave.
It was engineered by Joaquim Cardozo and dedicated on 31 May 1970.

architects.name: Oscar Niemeyer
architects.bio: Born in Rio de Janeiro, Niemeyer turned reinforced concrete into free, sensual curves, from the Pampulha ensemble of the 1940s to the palaces of Brasília. Working until his death at 104, he received the Pritzker Prize in 1988 and became the best-known architect Brazil has produced.

image.alt: Corner of a building with tall concrete arches rising from a reflecting pool
image.credit: Photo: Ricardo Patiño · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Tall arches stand directly in the water.

hints.text: Inside, a spiral staircase with no central support seems to float between floors.

image.alt: Long arcade of slender concrete arches around a glass building, with a white sculpture in the pool
image.credit: Photo: Ricardo Patiño · CC BY-SA 2.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Brazil's Ministry of Foreign Affairs occupies a glass box surrounded by a colonnade of slender concrete arches that rise out of a reflecting pool, with gardens by Roberto Burle Marx. Technical difficulties delayed its completion until April 1970.
keyFeatures: Glass building inside a concrete arcade
Arches standing in a reflecting pool
Spiral staircase without central support
Gardens by Roberto Burle Marx
funFacts: It was first called the Palácio dos Arcos, the Palace of the Arches.
In front of it stands Meteoro, a marble sculpture by Bruno Giorgi.

name: Pinacoteca do Estado de São Paulo

architects.name: Ramos de Azevedo
aliases: Francisco de Paula Ramos de Azevedo
architects.bio: The most prolific architect of turn-of-the-century São Paulo, Ramos de Azevedo ran the office behind many of the city's public buildings and directed the Liceu de Artes e Ofícios, for which this building was designed.

architects.name: Domiziano Rossi
architects.bio: Ramos de Azevedo's main collaborator, who designed the Liceu building with him in the Italian eclectic manner.

architects.name: Paulo Mendes da Rocha
architects.bio: Born in Vitória and based in São Paulo, Mendes da Rocha was a leading figure of the Paulista School, known for bold, economical concrete structures. He received the Pritzker Prize in 2006 and the Venice Biennale's Golden Lion in 2016.

architects.name: Eduardo Colonelli
architects.bio: São Paulo architect who led the 1993–98 renovation with Paulo Mendes da Rocha and Weliton Ricoy Torres.

architects.name: Weliton Ricoy Torres
architects.bio: São Paulo architect, co-author of the 1993–98 renovation with Paulo Mendes da Rocha and Eduardo Colonelli.

image.alt: Corner of a building in bare red brick, seen from below
image.credit: Photo: Eugenio Hansen, OFS · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: The brick walls were never covered with the plaster that was planned.

hints.text: It was built for a school of arts and crafts and opened, still unfinished, in 1900.

image.alt: Long brick building with colonnaded loggias behind a garden fountain
image.credit: Photo: Wilfredor · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

hints.caption: Exterior

summary.description: Designed by Ramos de Azevedo and Domiziano Rossi for the Liceu de Artes e Ofícios, this eclectic brick building beside the Jardim da Luz opened unfinished in 1900 and became the home of São Paulo's oldest art museum, founded in 1905. Between 1993 and 1998 Paulo Mendes da Rocha, with Eduardo Colonelli and Weliton Ricoy Torres, transformed it: the courtyards were roofed with glass and crossed by metal walkways, and the bare brick was left on show.
keyFeatures: Exposed brick walls, never plastered
Two inner courtyards roofed in glass during the renovation
Metal walkways crossing the courtyards
Side loggias and windows facing the Jardim da Luz
funFacts: The renovation won the Mies van der Rohe Prize for Latin America.
It was listed as a heritage building in 1982, part of the turn-of-the-century ensemble of the Luz district.
